items.title: 8.4 Polarized light by the method of reflection

source_refs.note: Topic 8.4 with Fig. 8.6 and Example 8.1 (PDF 177-178, printed 174-175). 'Brewester' is a print misspelling of Brewster.

blocks.text: In 1808, Malus discovered that polarized light is obtained when ordinary light is reflected (light bouncing back from a surface) by a plane sheet of glass. If the reflected light is viewed through a polaroid which is slowly rotated about the line of vision, the light is practically extinguished at one position of the polaroid. The most suitable angle of incidence ‘i’ is about 57° for glass for which the reflected ray becomes plane polarized, as illustrated by ray diagram in Fig. (8.6). This proves that the light reflected by the glass is practically plane polarized. Light reflected from the surface of a table becomes darker when viewed through a rotated polaroid, showing that it is partially plane polarized.

blocks.alt: Ray diagram. Incident unpolarized light (vibrations in all directions) strikes the boundary between Medium 1 (n1, Air) and Medium 2 (n2, Crown glass, n = 1.52; n2 > n1) at i = theta_p = 57 degrees to the dashed normal. The reflected light, plane polarized, carries dots for its vibrations and is viewed through a polaroid. The refracted light at r = theta_r carries double arrows. Reflected and refracted rays are at 90 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.6: Plane polarization by reflection (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 8.6 draws the reflected, plane-polarized light with vibrations in all directions and an in-plane double arrow after the polaroid. Reflected light is polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence, drawn as dots above.

The particular angle of incidence on a transparent medium when the reflected light is almost plane polarized is called the polarizing angle. Let a beam of unpolarized light be made incident on the surface of medium 2 as shown in Fig.8.6. If the reflected beam of light is almost plane polarized, the reflected and refracted beams are at right angle to each other at the polarizing angle, i = θₚ. Thus

blocks.text_alt: n₁ sin θₚ = n₂ sin θᵣ
n₁ sin θₚ = n₂ sin(90° − θₚ)
n₂ sin θₚ = n₂ cos θₚ

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The third line of the derivation is printed with n₂ on both sides. From the line before it, n₁ sin θₚ = n₂ sin(90° − θₚ) = n₂ cos θₚ, so the line is n₁ sin θₚ = n₂ cos θₚ, which gives tan θₚ = n₂/n₁ below.

blocks.text_alt: sin θₚ / cos θₚ = n₂ / n₁

blocks.text: This equation is known as Brewster's law. In this equation, n₁ is refractive index of medium 1 and n₂ is refractive index of medium 2. If medium 1 is air, then equation becomes tanθₚ = n because n₁ = 1 and n₂ = n. Here n is refractive index of medium on which light is incident. Hence, Brewester proved that the tangent of the angle of polarization is numerically equal to the refractive index of the medium 2 when medium 1 is air. In Brewster's law, the angle ‘θₚ’ for which the reflected ray and refracted ray makes an angle of 90° between them, is also called the Brewster angle θ_B. Then tanθ_B = n holds.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Malus's law is used to study the polarization of light in biological systems, such as the polarization of light by cell membranes.

blocks.title: Example 8.1
blocks.problem: A beam of light strikes the surface of a plate of glass with a refractive index of √3 at the polarizing angle. What will be the angle of refraction of the wave of light?
